title: Five-Year Plans and the temples of modern India
paragraphs: Independent India’s first public-works generation was organised by the Planning Commission. The First Five-Year Plan (1951–56) put capital into irrigation and community development. The Second (1956–61), under P. C. Mahalanobis, shifted scarce foreign exchange toward steel, heavy electricals, and machine-building. Jawaharlal Nehru, opening Bhakra and other river-valley sites, called large dams the temples of a resurgent India. The phrase is over-quoted. The useful fact is that the Union chose a few river sites, a few mill towns, and a few campuses, and then lived with their political geography for seventy years.

Hirakud, Bhakra-Nangal, and Nagarjuna Sagar were planned as irrigation, power, and flood control together, in a Tennessee Valley manner that Indian engineers had studied before 1947. IIT Kharagpur opened in the buildings of the former Hijli Detention Camp in 1951. AIIMS was created by statute in 1956. These are public works in the same sense as a dam: Union capital, a named site, and a long afterlife. The map begins on 15 August 1947. Works begun under the colonial state and finished after that date — Hirakud, Bhakra, Tungabhadra, the Damodar Valley Corporation — are dated by both start and opening.

title: Irrigation, hydropower, and displacement
paragraphs: The river-valley project was independent India’s first industrial policy. Hirakud on the Mahanadi (inaugurated 1957), Bhakra on the Sutlej (1963), Nagarjuna Sagar on the Krishna (1967), and later Koyna, Idukki, Tehri, and Indira Sagar stored monsoon water for canals and turbines. The Indira Gandhi Canal carried Himalayan water into the Thar. The Kosi barrage and eastern canal were built with Nepal under a 1954 agreement. Farakka Barrage, dedicated in 1975, diverted Ganga water toward Kolkata Port and became a standing subject of the 1996 treaty with Bangladesh.

Displacement is part of that geography. Official household counts and campaign estimates do not agree, and this atlas does not average them. For Hirakud, later Odisha statements run from about 18,000 families and 111 fully submerged villages to more than 26,000 families and some 325 villages. THDC’s Tehri figures are given as families; Britannica states about 100,000 people. Sardar Sarovar, litigated for decades and dedicated in 2017, is the late member of the same family: who counted as a project-affected family, and at which dam height, was itself the dispute. Polavaram, declared a national project in 2014, remains unfinished; a CAG performance audit recorded 1,06,006 project-displaced families.

title: Steel towns and the public-sector plant
paragraphs: Rourkela, Bhilai, and Durgapur were the industrial urbanism of the Second Plan: a German plant, a Soviet plant, and a British plant, each with a company town. SAIL records Bhilai’s first iron in 1959 and Durgapur’s million-tonne stage in 1962. Bokaro’s first blast furnace was blown in 1972. Visakhapatnam Steel, a later public-sector mill, sold steel from 1990 and was commissioned in 1992. Heavy Engineering Corporation at Ranchi (1958) and BHEL’s Bhopal works (dedicated 1960) were meant to make the machines that made the mills.

The energy map then shifted west. Bombay High, discovered in 1974 and producing from May 1976, put ONGC on the Arabian Sea shelf. Mathura Refinery (1982) processed that crude for the north. Jamnagar, commissioned in 1999, is private. Ownership is recorded; it is not ranked. Kandla was built after Partition left Karachi in Pakistan. JNPT, commissioned in 1989, became the Union’s principal container port. The mills and the ports are one industrial geography, not two moral categories.

title: Highways, Konkan, and the metro template
paragraphs: The Golden Quadrilateral — about 5,846 km joining Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, and Mumbai — was Phase I of the National Highways Development Project. Atal Bihari Vajpayee laid a foundation in January 1999; the government announced completion in January 2012. The North–South and East–West corridors followed as Phase II. Konkan Railway, a 756 km ghat alignment from Roha to Thokur, opened to through trains on 26 January 1998. It is a new line, not a widening of the colonial trunk. The western Dedicated Freight Corridor began carrying trains on the Rewari–Madar section in January 2021; the Dadri–JNPT spine was still being closed when this record was compiled.

Calcutta Metro, first commercial on 24 October 1984 between Esplanade and Bhowanipore, remained the only metro in the country until Delhi Metro opened Shahdara–Tis Hazari on 24 December 2002. Delhi became the template: a special-purpose corporation, elevated and underground lines, and a claim to remake the commute. Bengaluru (2011), Mumbai (2014), and Chennai (2015) copied the form as city systems. USBRL put the Kashmir Valley on broad gauge in sections from 2009; Chenab Bridge and the Katra–Banihal tunnels completed through running in 2024–25.

title: From Tarapur to the desert parks
paragraphs: Tarapur’s two GE boiling-water reactors entered commercial operation on 28 October 1969. Rawatbhata followed in 1973 with Canadian CANDU design. After the 1974 nuclear test, Canadian cooperation ended; Kalpakkam, Narora, Kakrapar, and Kaiga are indigenous PHWR stations. Kudankulam, a later Russian VVER import on the Tirunelveli coast, was synchronised in 2013 and declared commercial on 31 December 2014. Local opposition delayed fuel loading. The map records the plant and the protest as separate facts.

NTPC Singrauli, the first super thermal station of the public sector, commissioned Unit I in February 1982 on Singrauli coal and Rihand water. Thumba launched a Nike-Apache sounding rocket on 21 November 1963; Sriharikota became the orbital range with a Rohini-125 on 9 October 1971. Bhadla Solar Park in Jodhpur district was reported at about 2,245 MW by March 2020. Pavagada, on leased farmland in Tumakuru district, reached about 2,050 MW in December 2019. The solar park is land, modules, and evacuation lines rather than a single turbine hall.

title: Concessions, programmes, and unfinished capitals
paragraphs: Liberalisation changed who built the gateway. Cochin International Airport, inaugurated in May 1999, was the first Indian airport constructed as a public–private partnership, with state equity and NRI shareholders. Bengaluru (2008) and Shamshabad (2008) were larger concession airports. Mundra berthed its first ship in October 1998 and later overtook several Union major ports by tonnage. Ennore, corporatised and opened to coal in 2001, was the first major port as a company. Vallarpadam’s container terminal received its first vessel in 2011. Terminal 3 at Delhi’s IGI, a DIAL concession, opened in July 2010.

Bharatmala Pariyojana, approved by the Cabinet on 24 October 2017, is a highway programme, not a single alignment, and is marked ongoing. Amaravati, founded on 22 October 2015 as Andhra Pradesh’s greenfield capital after bifurcation, was paused under a three-capital scheme, ordered resumed by the High Court, and restarted after the 2024 election; it has no opening year. Polavaram remains incomplete. Atal Setu, the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link, opened to traffic on 13 January 2024. The atlas distinguishes an asset that can be commissioned from a programme that cannot.
